angle: A real Christmas tree cost $64 on average in 2015 (Square and NCTA) and about $83.87 in 2025 (Finder's analysis of NCTA data), up about 31%. The reason is a clock, not greed: a tree takes eight to ten years to reach market height, and after the 2008 recession growers planted fewer trees, which squeezed supply a decade later. In 2026, supply is back: 91% of wholesale growers surveyed by the Real Christmas Tree Board say they won't raise wholesale prices.
paragraphs: In 2015, the average real Christmas tree in America cost {sixty-four dollars|$64}.
Last year, it was about {eighty-four dollars|$83.87}. Up almost a third.
Blame the clock. A tree takes {eight to ten years|8 to 10 years} to grow. So this year's price was planted a decade ago.
And during the 2008 recession, farmers planted fewer trees. Ten years later, the shortage hit the lots.
Now the forest has caught up. This year, {ninety-one percent|91%} of big growers say they won't raise wholesale prices.
Your tree's price was set years before you bought it. More on the channel.
